title: Magnonic Combinatorial Memory based on a network of coupled active ring circuits
authors: Mykhaylo Balinskiy, Paulo Julio, Jeffrey Vargas, Diana Bisono Balaguer, Jacob Greenstein, Alexander Khitun
abstract: Magnonic Combinatorial Memory (MCM) is a type of memory where the bits of information are encoded in the signal propagation paths in the network. In this work, we consider MCM based on the network of a coupled active ring circuit (ARC). Each circuit includes a broadband amplifier, a magnonic delay line, an adjustable frequency filter, an adjustable phase shifter, and a power detector. The coupling between the circuits is via spin waves propagating in the common delay line - ferrite film. There may or may not be auto-oscillations in the active ring circuits, depending on the combination of circuit parameters and circuit coupling. The address of MCM is defined as the combination of the states of the phase shifters and frequency filters, while the MCM state is defined as the presence/absence of the auto-oscillations. The coupling between the circuits is achieved by placing micromagnets on top of the ferrite film. The number of bits that can be encoded in the network increases quadratically with the number of coupled circuits. This scaling provides a fundamental advantage over conventional memory. We present experimental data obtained for three magnonic ARCs connected via a single-crystal yttrium iron garnet Y3Fe2(FeO4)3 (YIG) film. The data illustrate an example of encoding a 27-bit binary response pattern, corresponding to the 27 experimentally accessible phase combinations. The results demonstrate a robust operation of MCM with an On/Off ratio exceeding 30 dB at room temperature. The advantages and shortcomings of the proposed approach are discussed.
summary: This paper proposes a Magnonic Combinatorial Memory (MCM) that stores data by controlling the auto-oscillation state within a network of coupled active ring circuits. The system demonstrates a quadratic scaling of storage capacity with the number of coupled units, achieving high contrast ratios in experiments. It represents a solid-state approach to high-density, non-volatile memory using magnonics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the development of a novel, high-density memory device, the Magnonic Combinatorial Memory (MCM), whose information storage capacity scales quadratically with the number of coupled circuits.
main_result: Experimental demonstrations using three coupled active ring circuits achieved a 27-bit binary response pattern with a robust On/Off ratio exceeding 30 dB at room temperature.
method: The research combines theoretical modeling of coupled oscillator dynamics (using transfer matrices and spectral radius) with experimental characterization of magnonic circuits.
model_or_system: The system is based on a network of coupled Active Ring Circuits (ARCs) utilizing spin waves propagating in a Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) film. Information is encoded in the auto-oscillation state (presence/absence) determined by the phase and frequency settings of the coupled circuits.
key_observables: Auto-oscillation power (On/Off ratio), spectral radius ($ho(T)$), and the number of accessible phase combinations (bits).
important_parameters: Quadratic scaling of bits with the number of circuits ($O(N^2)$); On/Off ratio > 30 dB; Room temperature operation.
main_assumptions: The coupling mechanism is assumed reciprocal, and the analysis often relies on linearizing the dynamics or assuming independent control over coupling coefficients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of single and coupled ARCs, phase maps showing oscillation regions, and experimental data correlating phase settings with measured circulating power.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the MCM concept and its components (ARCs, coupling) to theoretical modeling of coupled dynamics, presenting experimental validation using multiple coupled circuits, and concluding with a discussion of scalability and limitations.
why_interesting: The use of coupled, non-linear, dissipative systems (ARCs) to store classical information via collective oscillation states provides a rich platform for studying non-equilibrium dynamics and complex state spaces, relevant to open quantum systems.
